ELSEVIER Tectonophysics 259 (1996) 259-284 
TECTONOPHYSICS 
Palaeomagnetism of Cretaceous to Tertiary sediments from 
southern Tibet: evidence for the extent of the northern margin of 
India prior to the collision with Eurasia 
A. Patzelt a,,, Huamei Li b, Junda Wang b, E. Appel a 
a lnstitutfiir Geologie und Paliiontologie, Universit~it 7"libingen, Sigwartstr. 10, 72076 T'tibingen, Germany 
b Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, PO Box 1131, Wushan, 51460 Guangzhou, China 
Received 2 December 1994; accepted ! November 1995 
Abstract 
Palaeomagnetic studies have been carried out on mid-Cretaceous to latest Palaeocene sediments from the Tethyan 
Himalaya on the northern margin of the Indian Plate near the localities of Gamba (28.3°N, 88.5°E) and Duela (28.0°N, 
89.2°E) in southern Tibet. A total of 61 sites (more than 700 cores) have been sampled mainly from limestones (Zongshan 
Formation, Jidula Formation Member II, Zongpu Formation), sandstones (Jidula Formation Member III) and graywackes 
(Gamba Group Member II), with ages well defined from detailed lithological and biostratigraphic analyses. Carriers of 
characteristic remanences are magnetite in limestones and graywackes, and hematite in sandstones. Reliable palaeodirections 
were obtained from 35 sites (356 specimens). Positive fold tests, antiparallel normal and reverse polarities, a northward trend 
of the palaeolatitudes with decreasing age, and absence of any metamorphic overprint indicate a primary origin for the 
characteristic remanences. 
The results have been compared with expected palaeodirections according to available data for the Indian subcontinent 
based on its present-day geometry. The late Maastrichtian sites (fourteen sites, 156 specimens) and the middle-Late 
Palaeocene sites (fourteen sites, 113 specimens) yield palaeolatitudes of 5.7°S and 4.0°N for the sampling localities in 
southern Tibet, respectively. These palaeolatitudes are much further north than expected and imply that crustal shortening 
between the Tethyan Himalaya and the Indian Shield since the time of India-Eurasia collision has occurred on the order of 
1500 km at the longitude of Gamba/Duela. Comparison of our observed palaeolatitudes with palaeolatitudes for the Lhasa 
block during Cretaceous and Palaeocene times indicate that initial contact of the northern Indian margin with the Lhasa 
block was already established at 65-60 Ma with suturing completed at about 55-50 Ma. 
I. Introduction 
The India-Eurasia convergence is well docu- 
mented by apparent polar wander paths (APWP) for 
both continents (Klootwijk, 1984; Besse and Cour- 
* Corresponding author. 
0040-1951/96/$15.00 Published by Elsevier Science B.V. 
SSDI 0040-1951(95)00181-6 
tillot, 1988, 1991). The separation of the Indian Plate 
from Gondwana started in mid- to Late Cretaceous 
times by opening of the Indian ocean at a moderate 
southern latitude. During the Late Cretaceous to 
Eocene India drifted northward over about 4000 km 
with drift rates up to 15-20 cm/yr. The drift is well 
documented from analyses of magnetic anomalies

from the Indian ocean (McKenzie and Sclater, 1971; 
Klootwijk and Peirce, 1979; Patriat and Achache, 
1984; Klootwijk et al., 1985; Royer and Sandwell, 
1989). A significant drop in the drift rate from nearly 
20 to less than 5 cm/yr at 55-50 Ma is mostly 
interpreted as the onset of the collision of the Indian 
Plate with the Eurasian Plate (e.g., Patriat and 
Achache, 1984; Besse and Courtillot, 1988). The 
initial collision occurred in the western part with 
progressive closure of the Neo-Tethyan ocean from 
west to east (Klootwijk et al., 1985). Further conver- 
gence led to straightforward and rotational under- 
thrusting of the Indian Plate beneath the southern 
Eurasian margin since the Miocene. During the past 
years an earlier age for the collision has been pro- 
posed. Based on a review of primary and secondary 
palaeoremanences from the Himalaya and Hin- 
dukush and results from the Ninetyeast Ridge, 
Klootwijk et al. (1991, 1992) concluded that initial 
contact between India and Eurasia was already estab- 
lished at the Cretaceous/Tertiary time boundary. 
They interpret the drop in drift rate at 55-50 Ma as 
completion of closure of the Neo-Tethys. Occurrence 
of high-pressure rocks of eclogite facies in the Upper 
Kaghan Valley (northwestern Himalaya) with a peak 
metamorphic age of 49_ 6 Ma (Tonarini et al., 
1993; Spencer, 1993) supports the hypothesis of an 
initial collision as early as 65 Ma in the western part. 
A vertebrate fauna with distinct Laurasian affinities 
found in intertrappean sediments, interbedded in the 
Deccan traps (Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary) give 
evidence for such an early contact (Prasad and Sahni, 
1988; Jaeger et al., 1989). 
Models for the mechanism of the India-Eurasia 
collision and for crustal shortening within the colli- 
sion zone have been proposed by many authors (e.g., 
Powell and Conaghan, 1973; Le Fort, 1975; Seeber 
et al., 1981; Tapponnier et al., 1982; Allegre et al., 
1984; Patriat and Achache, 1984; Klootwijk et al., 
1985, 1991; Powell, 1986; Tapponnier et al., 1986; 
Dewey et al., 1988; Chen et al., 1993b). Crustal 
shortening through imbricate stacking within the Hi- 
malayan crust, underplating of the Indian Plate be- 
neath Eurasia, thickening of the Eurasian crust 
through plastic deformation and folding, and east- 
ward extrusion of continental blocks within southern 
Eurasia are discussed. For quantitative reconstruc- 
tions and for dating of the initial contact, knowledge 
about the extent of the former northern margin of 
India, the so-called Greater India (Veevers et al., 
1975), is essential. The Tethyan Himalaya, as the 
former northern margin of the Indian Plate plays a 
key role in reconstructions of Greater India, palaeo- 
magnetic data from this zone, however, are quite 
rare. Results have been published by Klootwijk and 
Bingham (1980), Klootwijk et al. (1983), Zhu Zhi- 
wen and Teng Jiwen (1984), Besse et al. (1984) and 
Appel et al. (1991, 1995), but only a single study 
(Tingri, 29°N, 87°E, Besse et al., 1984) details a 
palaeoremanence with an acquisition age within the 
particularly important period of rapid northward drift 
of India. Apart from Tingri, Late Cretaceous-Eocene 
marine Tethyan sediments are found only in Zanskar 
(34°N, 76.5°E) and in the area around Gamba and 
Duela (28°N, 89°E) (see Fig. l a). Intensive palaeo- 
magnetic investigations in Zanskar (Appel et al., 
1995) yielded a well established secondary palaeore- 
manence, but no primary component. 
Results from the Tethyan Himalaya of Gamba and 
Duela are presented here for middle Albian-Late 
Palaeocene rocks and provide information on palaeo- 
latitudes and rotations of the northernmost part of 
Greater India prior to and during the early stages of 
the collision of India with Eurasia. 
2. Geology and sampling 
The principal tectonic units of the Himalaya are 
shown in Fig. la. The suture zone (IYS: Indus 
Yarlung suture) between India and Eurasia is marked 
by ophiolites along the rivers Indus and Yarlung. 
During further convergence the active zone of sub- 
duction propagated southward leading to continental 
underthrusting along the Main Central Thrust (MCT) 
in Oligocene-Miocene times, subsequently along the 
Fig. 1. (a) Schematic map of the Himalaya (simplified after Gansser, 1964). The localities with Late Cretaceous-Eocene marine Tethyan 
sediments are marked by stars. Z = Zanskar; T = Tingri; G = Gamba; D = Duela+ (b) Tectonostratigraphic map of the investigation area 
(after Liu, 1992). GKT = Gyirong-Kangmar thrust; TGT = Tingri-northern Gamba thrust.

### page_5
A. Patzelt et al. / Tectonophysics 259 (1996) 259-284 263 
Main Boundary Fault (MBF) (e.g., Le Fort, 1975), 
and finally along the presently active Main Frontal 
Thrust (Gansser, 1991). The Tethyan Himalaya as 
the former leading edge of Greater India is now 
situated directly south of the IYS. The sedimentary 
sequences of the Tethyan zone were deposited as 
shelf sediments on the northern margin of the Indian 
continent from Precambrian to Eocene times. 
Our sampling areas near Gamba (28.3°N, 88.5°E) 
and Duela (28.0°N, 89.3°E) are shown in Fig. lb. In 
the Gamba area a continuous sedimentary succession 
from late Aptian to Early Eocene is well preserved 
(Gansser, 1964; Wen, 1987a,b; Willems and Zhang, 
1993). A detailed lithological and biostratigraphic 
description of this succession is given by Willems 
and Zhang (1993). No signs of metamorphism are 
found within these sediments and occurrence of 
anatas (TiO 2 modification) in the Jidula sandstones 
of Gamba and Duela proves that heating did not 
exceed 260°C (J. Schaller, pets. commun., 1994). 
Our work focused on the Albian-Palaeocene suc- 
cessions, deposited during the rapid northward drift 
of India prior to and during the onset of collision. 
The mid-Cretaceous-Palaeocene succession of the 
type section at Gamba is shown in Fig. 2. It can be 
divided into four lithostratigraphic units: the Gamba 
Group (Neocomian-Santonian), the Zongshan For- 
mation (Campanian-Maastrichtian), the Jidula For- 
mation (latest Maastrichtian-Early Palaeocene) and 
the Zongpu Formation (middle Palaeocene-latest 
Palaeocene). The Gamba Group can be divided into 
three members and consists of gray shales with

(b) Local map of Duela (28.0°N, 89.2°E).

### page_6
264 A. Patzelt et al. / Tectonophysics 259 (1996) 259-284 
interbedded marls, sandstones and limestones. The 
overlying Zongshan Formation consists of three 
scarp-forming limestone units with interbedded cal- 
careous marls. It is very rich in fossils, allowing 
excellent biostratigraphic classification. The Jidula 
Formation is built up mainly by sandstones, with a 
dark limestone layer intercalated in Member II. The 
Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary occurs within this 
formation. Its exact position, however, is unclear due 
to the lack of biostratigraphically significant fossils 
in the sandstones. The Zongpu Formation consists 
mainly of massive limestone beds, nodular lime- 
stones and calcareous marls. Planktonic foraminifera 
of the Angulata Zone indicate a middle Palaeocene 
age for the lower part of the Zongpu Formation. The 
occurrence of Alveolina, Orbitolites and small Num- 
mulites in Member IV, the top of the Zongpu Forma- 
tion, give a classification into the Ilerdian. The 
Palaeocene/Eocene boundary lies within the overly- 
ing Zongpubei Formation, which consists of greenish 
marls and red claystones and siltstones. The lithos- 
tratigraphy of the Late Cretaceous-Palaeocene suc- 
cession in Duela is generally comparable to that of 
Gamba (Pfl~isterer et al., 1993). However, the Jidula 
limestone layer is not exposed at Duela. 
Sampling was carried out in the summers of 1986 
and 1992 as part of Chinese-German joint projects 
for study of the Cretaceous/Tertiary stratigraphy 
and evolution of the Tethyan Himalaya in southern 
Tibet. A portable rockdrill was used for sampling, 
and the cores were oriented with a magnetic com- 
pass. The generally weak intensity of magnetization 
in the rocks did not require the use of a solar 
compass. Usually ten cores of 2.5 cm diameter were 
taken from each site. A total of more than 700 
oriented samples from 61 sites were drilled from the 
above mentioned four stratigraphic units of mid- 
Cretaceous-latest Palaeocene age at Gamba and Du- 
ela. No samples could be taken from the highly 
weathered Eocene Zongpubei Formation. The strati- 
graphic positions of the sites are shown in Fig. 2. 
Local maps of the sampling areas together with the 
exact site locations are shown in Fig. 3a and b. 
3. Sample treatment 
The core samples were cut into specimens with a 
length of 2.2-2.3 cm. For analyses of the ferrimag- 
netic minerals one specimen per site was used for 
isothermal remanence acquisition (IRM) studies in a 
DC field up to 1.5 T with subsequent stepwise 
thermal demagnetization of the saturation IRM 
(SIRM). Detailed stepwise alternating field (AF) and

Fig. 4. Acquisition and thermal demagnetization curves of isother-

### page_7
A. Patzelt et al. / Tectonophysics 259 (1996) 259-284 265 
thermal demagnetization (TH) was carried out on 
pilot specimens from each site. Susceptibility was 
monitored after each heating step to detect possible 
mineralogical alterations. Depending on the results 
of the pilot studies and the IRM curves, the remain- 
ing specimens of all sites were demagnetized accord- 
ing to the best suitable procedure; that is either 
thermally (MTDM1 and Schonstedt furnaces), or in 
alternating fields (using 2G and Highmoor AF de- 
magnetizers), or a combination of both methods. 
Remanence directions were measured with cryogenic 
magnetometers (R6manombtre h Squid RS 01, LETI, 
noise level about 0.02 mA/m; 2G 755 R, noise level 
< 0.01 mA/m). Orthogonal vector plots and equal 
area projections were used to examine the behaviour 
of the specimens upon demagnetization. Magnetic 
directions were mainly (> 70%) determined from 
straight segments of the demagnetization paths 
through principal component analysis (PCA, modi- 
fied version after Kirschvink, 1980), and in part 
(< 30%) from stable end directions. Calculations of 
mean values were done applying Fisherian statistics 
(Fisher, 1953)• 
4. Palaeomagnetic results 
The results from both sampling localities, Gamba 
and Duela, are discussed together for each lithostrati- 
graphic unit, because their rock magnetic properties 
and demagnetization behaviour are very similar. 
4.1. The Gamba Group (Member II) 
Magnetite is the only ferrimagnetic mineral indi- 
cated by the low coercivity forces and the unblock- 
ing temperatures of about 570°C (Fig. 4a). There- 
fore, the bulk of the specimens were AF demagne- 
tized. Typically a two-component behaviour could be 
observed (Fig. 5a and b). A soft, randomly oriented 
magnetic remanence was completely removed at peak 
fields of 5-20 mT. Statistical data for the remaining 
characteristic remanence (ChRM) directions are listed 
in Table 1. Both sampled sites yielded significant 
results. The single specimen directions for the ChRM 
and the in situ directions for the soft component are 
shown in Fig. 6. The site mean values are plotted in 
Fig. 13. 
4.2. The Zongshan Formation 
Nearly all sites show IRM acquisition curves (Fig. 
4b) with a lower coercivity component (exception 
sites A26, D40) that is in many cases coexisting with 
a high coercivity component. Thermal demagnetiza- 
tion of the SIRM (Fig. 4b) and NRM (Fig. 7e) 
reveals unblocking temperatures for the two compo- 
nents up to 450-580°C and 675°C, respectively,

Analyses of directional data show a two-component 
behaviour. During AF demagnetization (Fig. 7a) a 
soft component with an in situ direction parallel to 
the local ambient field is removed up to about 15 
mT. A second, harder component is demagnetized 
between 20 and 100 mT, with the demagnetization 
path pointing to the origin. A similar two-component

Fig. 8. Equal area projection of individual specimen directions from the Zongshan Formation. (a) In situ soft components. (b) Tilt corrected 
ChRM directions, (c) In situ ChRM directions from members II, Ill, IV. (d) In situ soft components. (e) Tilt corrected ChRM directions. (f) 
In situ ChRM directions from Member I. The present dipole field direction is shown as a rhomb in (a), (c), (d) and (f). 
behaviour is observed during thermal treatment (Fig. 
7b), but the demagnetization path is less smooth. The 
soft component is removed up to about 350°C, the 
hard component up to about 530°C. Generally a 
major increase in susceptibility is observed above 
450°C. The bulk of the specimens from the Zong- 
shan Formation were therefore first heated up to 
150°C in order to destroy possible goethite rema- 
nences and subsequently AF demagnetized in fields 
up to 100 mT. The hard AF component was taken as 
the ChRM. In some specimens only a single compo- 
nent behaviour was observed (Fig. 7c). In the case of 
low median destructive fields (MDF) < 10 mT, the 
specimens were rejected from further calculations. 
Single components with a high MDF > 15 mT were 
accepted as representing the ChRM (Fig. 7c, the 
magnetization intensity remaining after the 150°C 
step is taken as the initial value for calculating the 
MDF). 
The demagnetization behaviour together with IRM 
curves prove magnetite as the carrier of the ChRM. 
The high stability of this harder magnetite compo- 
nent upon AF demagnetization (Fig. 7a-d) suggests 
a single-domain (SD) or pseudo-single-domain (PSD) 
status of this magnetite fraction. Hematite does not 
contribute significantly to the total remanence. In 
cases of weak NRM intensities a residual hematite 
component is partially observed after the maximum 
step of demagnetization. However, ChRM directions 
at 20 mT (dominated by magnetite) do not signifi- 
cantly differ from the stable residual directions at 
100 mT (mainly carried by hematite). 
Statistical data for ChRM directions are listed in 
Table 2 for the Gamba sites and in Table 3 for the 
Duela sites. Fifteen of the 27 treated sites yielded 
significant results. The in situ directions of the soft 
component and the single specimen directions of the 
ChRM are plotted in Fig. 8. The site mean values are 
plotted in Fig. 13. Rejected sites either show a 
present field direction only, or a high scattering of 
remanence directions. The implications of the oppos- 
ing mainly normal and exclusively reverse polarities 
in the Gamba and Duela sites, respectively, will be 
discussed below. 
4.3. The Jidula Formation 
The lithologic differences of Jidula members I 
and III (sandstones) and Jidula Member II (limes- 
tones) result in a different magnetic mineralogy. 
Hematite is predominant in the sandstones with 
additional goethite and magnetite in some of the

### page_12
270 A. Patzelt et al. / Tectonophysics 259 (1996) 259-284 
specimens [identified mainly by unblocking tempera- 
tures above 600°C, at about 100°C and at about 
300-500°C, respectively (Fig. 4c, specimen B30; 
Fig. 9a-c)]. After removal of goethite remanences 
through heating above 100°C, remanence directions 
remained stable up to about 650°C (Fig. 9a and b). 
ChRM directions, carried by hematite (and probably 
also by magnetite in some of the specimens) were 
determined from demagnetization data obtained after 
the 200°C heating step. 
In the limestones magnetite is dominant with a 
minor hematite component, identified by low coer- 
civity combined with unblocking temperatures < 
around 500°C and high coercivity combined with 
unblocking temperatures > 600°C, respectively (Fig. 
4c, specimen B8). AF demagnetization usually re- 
vealed two components (Fig. 9d-f). After removal of 
a soft component with scattered directions a harder 
component is demagnetized between 20 and 100 mT. 
This hard component is taken as the ChRM, similar 
to the Zongshan Formation. The ChRM could be 
determined from most of the specimens. As it was 
the case for the Zongshan limestones hematite does 
not contribute significantly to the total remanence. 
Statistical data for the ChRM directions are listed 
in Table 4. Individual specimen directions for the 
ChRM component and also for the soft component 
of the limestones are shown in Fig. 10. The site 
mean values are plotted in Fig. 13. Reliable results 
are obtained from four sites (three limestone, one 
sandstone) from the Gamba area. With the exception 
of one site, the sandstones show highly scattered

extension of about 500 m. 
4.4. The Zongpu Formation 
IRM curves (Fig. 4d) and demagnetization be- 
haviour (Fig. 11) are similar to the Zongshan Forma- 
tion. Low and high coercivity forces and unblocking 
temperatures of 400-500°C and 675°C indicate mag- 
netite and hematite as ferrimagnetic minerals. 
Goethite also occurs in several sites. 
Similar to the Zongshan Formation the suscepti- 
bility increased during thermal demagnetization 
above about 450°C. The bulk of the specimens was 
demagnetized in alternating fields up to 100 mT after 
a single heating step at 120 or 150°C. A soft compo- 
nent, parallel to the local ambient field, was then 
removed up to 15 mT. A very well determined 
harder component was demagnetized between 20 and 
100 mT, with a demagnetization path pointing to the 
origin. This component is interpreted as the ChRM 
direction (Fig. 1 la and b). The high stability of the 
hard component upon AF demagnetization (Fig. 1 lc) 
indicates a SD or PSD domain status of this mag- 
netite fraction. Similar to the Zongshan Formation 
magnetite is the carrier of the ChRM and rema- 
nences carried by hematite seem to be negligible. 
Statistical data for the ChRM directions are listed 
in Table 5 (Gamba) and Table 6 (Duela). Fourteen of 
the 23 treated sites yielded reliable results. Detailed 
stratigraphic control allows us to divide the results 
from Gamba in a "lower" (middle Palaeocene) and 
"upper" (Late Palaeocene)Zongpu Group with four 
and six sites, respectively (see also Fig. 2). Individ- 
ual specimen directions for the ChRM and the soft 
component are plotted in Fig. 12. The site mean 
directions are plotted in Fig. 13. Sites were rejected 
if they showed either a present field direction only 
(mainly due to low NRM intensities), or a high 
scatter of remanence directions.

eight groups (Tables 7 and 8; Fig. 13).

### page_18
276 A. Patzelt et al. / Tectonophysics 259 (1996) 259-284 
tion at the sampling area does not lie within the ot.95 
circle around the ChRM site mean values in situ 
(with exception of site B86-S, sandstone from the 
Jidula Formation), and (2) stable PSD/SD magnetite 
is identified as the predominant cartier of the ChRM. 
Several arguments support primary origin for the 
ChRM: (3) Antiparallel normal and reverse polarities 
are observed from the Zongshan, Jidula and Zongpu 
formations. The observed polarities are in agreement 
with the magnetic polarity time scale (Fig. 14, after 
Ogg, 1995), namely, normal polarity for the Albian 
Gamba Group Member II, mixed polarity for the 
Maastrichtian Zongshan Formation, reverse polarity 
for the Jidula Member II (deposited around the Cre- 
taceous/Tertiary time boundary), predominantly 
normal polarity for the subsequent Jidula Member III 
and nearly exclusively reverse polarity for the mid- 
dle-Late Palaeocene Zongpu Formation. (4) Palaeo- 
latitudes show a northward progress with decreasing 
rock age as is expected from the northward drift of 
India. (5) No signs of metamorphism could be de- 
tected in the sampled units. (6) A positive fold test 
(McElhinny, 1964) is obtained for the Zongshan 
Formation (members II, III and IV) that is significant 
at the 99% level with ktilt cor/kin situ = 4.28 (N = 14 
sites). Due to the rather uniform bedding dip, the 
high significance of the fold test depends mainly on 
site A23 and on its correct polarity interpretation 
(Table 7; Fig. 13). Site A23 was drilled on an 
overturned limb of a S-vergent fold. The structure 
has been well established through detailed tectonic 
observations (Burda, 1993). Ten out of a total of 
eleven treated specimens from site A23 yielded a 
ChRM direction. The in situ ChRM directions ob- 
tained from the overturned bedding of site A23 are 
all reverse, whereas the in situ ChRM directions

Fig. 14. Magnetic polarity time scale (after Ogg, 1995) plotted 
together with possible ranges of remanence ages according to rock 
ages and polarities of ChRM directions. 
from all other -- normally bedded -- specimens 
from the Zongshan Formation are exclusively of 
normal polarity. Hence, it seems to be a fairly reli- 
able fact that the observed reverse polarity of the 
ChRM directions of site A23 is due to the overturned 
bedding. If site A23 is excluded, the ktilt cor//kin situ 
becomes 0.93, and the fold test is no longer signifi- 
cant. All Zongpu Formation sites show a fold test 
that is significant at the 95% level (ktilt cor//kin 
situ = 2.10, for N= 14 sites), but is based on sites 
with only moderately different bedding (Fig. 13). 
Fold tests for the Gamba Group and the Jidula 
Formation are not significant due to the uniform 
bedding dip and the small number of sites. Partial 
unfolding tests were not applied, because the data 
seem not to be sufficient (in terms of different 
bedding attitudes) and because Tauxe and Watson 
(1994) showed that possible block rotations around 
subvertical axes could lead to misinterpretations. 
The high drift rate of India of up to 20 cm/yr 
requires detailed control of the remanence acquisi- 
tion ages in order to allow a comparison of our data 
with an APWP for India. Biostratigraphic dating of 
the sites is very accurate (Willems and Zhang, 1993) 
and further information is provided by the magnetic 
polarity observed for the sites (Fig. 13). The ChRM 
directions of the Zongshan Formation of Gamba all 
show a normal polarity. Biostratigraphic control 
places the transition from Campanian to Maas- 
trichtian within the calcareous marls on top of Lime- 
stone I. Consequently the magnetization of the Zong- 
shan Formation (members II and III) of Gamba must 
have been acquired within either Chron 30N or 31N. 
Magnetostratigraphy alone does not allow to further 
constrain the Maastrichtian age for the reverse polar- 
ity results from the Zongshan Formation at Duela. It 
is surprising, that the Zongshan ChRM directions 
from Gamba and Duela show opposing polarities. 
We are not able to give a simple explanation here. 
The Late Cretaceous-Palaeocene formations at Du- 
ela are in general comparable to those at Gamba, but 
there are some differences in detail. The uppermost 
part of the Zongshan Formation at Gamba is made 
up of calcareous marls with a Rhodolite facies, 
whereas it is formed by a limestone layer IV (sites 
D44, D47 and D48) at Duela. The reverse polarity of 
the corresponding ChRM directions magnetization 
could have been acquired during either Chron 29R or 
30R. Sites D39, D42 and D53 are from the limestone 
layer II and their magnetization could have been 
acquired during Chron 31R or 30R. The limestone 
layer of the Jidula Formation was deposited around 
the Cretaceous/Tertiary time boundary and shows a 
reverse polarity for all specimens. Therefore the 
magnetization was acquired during Chron 28R or 
29R. The predominantly normal polarity ChRM of 
the subsequent Jidula Member III is interpreted to 
correspond with Chron 28N or 29N. Correlations 
with the magnetic polarity time scale provide no 
further information in the case of the various Zongpu

### page_20
278 A. Patzelt et al. / Tectonophysics 259 (1996) 259-284 
groups (predominantly reverse polarities) and the 
Albian Gamba Group within the Cretaceous normal 
polarity Super-Chron C34N. 
5. Discussion 
In order to reconstruct the northern extent of 
Greater India prior to collision with southern Asia 
and to estimate the magnitude of crustal shortening, 
observed palaeolatitudes are compared with expected 
palaeolatitudes for the locality of Gamba, Expected 
palaeolatitude reference curves are calculated from 
available data for stable India based on the present- 
day geography (Table 9). Different reference curves 
result from the Master APWP (REF A) published by 
Besse and Courtillot (1991), simulated pole positions 
(REF B) listed in Klootwijk et al. (1991) and palaeo- 
magnetic results from the Ninetyeast Ridge (Kloot- 
wijk et al., 1991, 1992). Expected and observed (our

data) palaeolatitudes are plotted in Fig. 15 with their 
confidence limits (dp values). The Master APWP 
results from selected palaeomagnetic data from 
Africa, Eurasia, North America (all transferred to 
India) and India using independent 20 myr time 
windows. The A95 values for the so calculated (REF 
A) Indian pole positions are relatively high for the 
time period 70-50 Ma, which is not surprising due 
to the high drift rate of India at that time. The 
simulated pole positions (REF B) are derived from 
India-Africa relative movement with Africa fixed to 
a hot spat frame. They are based on an updated set 
of magnetic anomaly analyses, similar to that of 
Patriat and Achache (1984). The error estimate for 
these pole positions is about +3 ° (Patriat and 
Achache, 1984). 
Palaeopositions of our data fall significantly to the 
north of the three sets of expected palaeolatitudes. 
The difference can be interpreted as the minimum 
magnitude of crustal shortening between the Tethyan 
Himalaya and the Indian Shield at the longitude of 
the sampling sites (88.5°E) since the time of rema- 
nence acquisition. The crustal shortening results are:

assumed to be +__ 6 ° for REF A and + 3 ° for REF B, 
errors of observed palaeolatitudes are presented as 
dp equivalents to a95 values, uncertainties in age not 
regarded). The Gamba Group and the Jidula Forma- 
tion are not considered because of the few sites (and 
specimens) only and an insufficient distribution of 
site localities. The calculated magnitudes of crustal 
shortening are valid for pure N-S-directed conver- 
gence. They are an underestimate if an E-W-di- 
rected component of crustal shortening has occurred, 
and they are also an underestimate if rotational short- 
ening is considered to contribute to the total magni- 
tude of crustal shortening. The Indian Shield rotated 
about 20 ° counterclockwise since the Late Creta- 
ceous, whereas the mean declination of all sites from 
the Zongshan and Zongpu formations at our refer- 
ence locality Gamba is about 0 °. This difference can 
be explained by rotational shortening following the 
oroclinal bending model of Klootwijk et al. (1985). 
The observed palaeodeclination can be transferred to 
an orientation parallel to the expected one by recon-

### page_23
A. Patzelt et al. / Tectonophysics 259 (1996) 259-284 281 
struction of the Himalayan arc into a straight line 
and an additional rotation of this straight segment. 
The model is not unambiguous, however, for the 
longitude of Gamba, the path of rotational crustal 
shortening can be approximated by the arc of circle 
from Gex p to G' around a pivot at 35°N, 73°E 
(according to Klootwijk et al., 1985) (Fig. 16a). A 
magnitude of rotational shortening of about 600 km 
at the longitude of Gamba results from our data. This 
value is in agreement with earlier results published 
by Klootwijk et al. (1985) and Appel et al. (1991). 
The path Gexo-G' involves a minor E-W-directed 
component of shortening at the longitude of Gamba 
(Fig. 16a). Provided that no other E-W-directed 
component of crustal shortening has occurred, the 
residual difference of palaeolatitudes between G' and 
Gob s results in a further straightforward shortening in 
N-S direction (Fig. 16a), that can be seen as uniform 
Himalayan-wide shortening. The path Gcxo-G'-Gobs 
in Fig. 16a defines the minimum magnitude of crustal 
shortening (approximately 1500 km), but this is cer- 
tainly based on a simplified model. Of course, 
straightforward and rotational crustal shortening are 
likely to have occurred simultaneously. 
It is generally accepted that crustal shortening 
within Greater India occurred by underthrusting 
(mainly along the MCT) and internal deformation 
(folding and thrusting). Strong evidence for whole- 
sale underthrusting of Indian crust beneath the 
Tethyan Himalaya is provided from recent deep seis- 
mic reflection profiling beneath southern Tibet (Zhao 
et al., 1993; Nelson et al., 1995). Palaeomagnetic 
estimates of the magnitude of crustal shortening 
between stable India and the Tethyan Himalaya vary 
between 700 km (Patriat and Achache, 1984), 1000 
km (Dewey et al., 1989; Chen et al., 1993b) and a 
minimum of 1000 km (Klootwijk et al., 1985) for the 
eastern parts of India. Our result of about 1500 km 
crustal shortening exceed these values, but is based 
on an extensive new data set. Of course there re- 
mains the problem of error determination, and the 
lower 95% confidence limit of crustal shortening 
from our data (about 1000 km) is still in agreement 
with the other results mentioned above. 
The only previously published palaeomagnetic re- 
sult from Tethyan Himalayan rocks within the period 
Late Cretaceous-Eocene by Besse et al. (1984) from 
Tingri (see Fig. la) yields a palaeolatitude of 2.5°S 
___ 4 ° for the eastern Tethyan Himalaya at 57 Ma. 
Crustal shortening on the order of 400 km along the 
MCT and MBF was inferred by the authors. The 
result of Besse et al. (1984) is based on primary 
remanences of three limestone sites (22 specimens 
only) and one sandstone site (six specimens). Exclu- 
sion of the sandstone site result (which seems to be 
questionable) yields a palaeolatitude of 2.3°S -t- 7.3 °, 
undistinguishable from the original value but with a 
considerably increased confidence range. Further- 
more, palaeomagnetic investigations of Palaeocene 
and Eocene Tethyan sediments from the same Tingri 
area (twelve sites with about 130 specimens, mostly 
limestones), carried out by our own group, show 
secondary remanences only (Appel et al., submitted). 
The confidence range of the result of Besse et al. 
(1984) includes the equator, and inclination shallow- 
ing could account for a palaeolatitude too close to 
the equator. Inclination shallowing can never be 
ruled out. However, if it occurred to our data from 
Gamba and Duela the difference between expected 
and observed palaeolatitudes would increase further. 
The magnitude of about 1500 km crustal shorten- 
ing demands also a discussion of the evolution of the 
northern margin of Greater India. Recent palaeogeo- 
graphic reconstructions for Gondwana, like that of 
Scotese (1991), show an oceanic gap up to about 
1000 km between northeastern India and northwest- 
ern Australia during Late Jurassic and Early Creta- 
ceous times. This gap disappears, assuming an ini- 
tially Greater India. An increase of the northern 
extent of Greater India might have been produced by 
extension of the Tethyan shelf (crustal thinning) 
during the rapid north drift, especially when the shelf 
came close to the subduction zone. Slab pull is 
indeed believed to act as a dominant force for the 
movement of the Indian Plate (Patriat and Achache, 
1984). The great diversification in the Late Creta- 
ceous-Palaeocene facies of the Tethyan Himalaya in 
the Zanskar area, with formation of blocks and basins, 
supports such an extension model for the shelf area 
as pointed out by Fuchs and Willems (1990). We can 
not distinguish from our data between models with 
or without extension, and palaeomagnetic data in 
general are not very adequate to do that. The strong 
counterclockwise rotation of the Indian Plate since 
the separation from Gondwana enlarge the confi- 
dence limits far above the resolution needed for

### page_24
282 A. Patzelt et al. / Tectonophysics 259 (1996) 259-284 
unequivocal conclusions. Nevertheless, comparison 
of palaeolatitudes calculated from the Gamba Group 
Member II and site A86-I (Zongshan Formation, 
Member I) with palaeolatitudes calculated from REF 
A at least indicates an already existing Greater India 
in the middle Albian and the early Campanian. The 
observed palaeopositions for our reference point 
Gamba are 23.6°/2600 km (Gamba Group) and 
11.7°/1300 km (A86-I) north of the expected ones. 
A very simple estimate of volume balancing doc- 
uments that 1500 km of crustal shortening at the 
northern margin of India are possible in principle. 
The sediments deposited in Himalayan foreland 
basins, fans and deltas account for 2 × 10 7 km 3 of 
eroded material (Johnson, 1994), derived mainly from 
the Higher Himalayan area with minor contributions 
from the Lesser Himalaya, Tibet and Karakoram. 
Most of these sediments, about 1.25 × 10 7 km 3, are 
stored in the Bengal fan (Curray, 1994). Another 
2 × 10 7 km 3 of material is stored in the 70 km thick 
Himalayan crust (Johnson, 1994). With an initial 
thinned Indian crust of 20-25 km thickness, as 
assumed by Dewey et al. (1989), this accounts for a 
block of about 1100 km length (with an E-W width 
of 2000 km for the subduction zone). Furthermore, 
the Indian slab was subducted beneath southern Ti- 
bet by a minimal length of 220-400 km (Patriat and 
Achache, 1984; Harrison et al., 1992; Zhao et al., 
1993; Nelson et al., 1995). This leads to a total of up 
to 1500 km of crustal shortening, without necessarily 
requiring an unlikely high magnitude of underplating 
of the Indian crust beneath Tibet or subduction of 
continental crust. 
Implications of our data on the timing of collision 
of Greater India with Eurasia also require control on 
the palaeoposition of the southern margin of Eurasia. 
The Master APWP for Eurasia (Besse and Courtillot, 
1991) would yield a Palaeocene palaeolatitude of 
28.5°N for the southern margin of stable Eurasia (at 
the longitude 88.5°E) based on the present-day geog- 
raphy. The southern edge of Eurasia was formed by 
the Lhasa block at that time. Comparison with palae- 
olatitude observations from this Lhasa block indicate 
post-collisional shortening of about 2000 km 
throughout southern Asia, comparable to the magni- 
tude calculated by Patriat and Achache (1984) on the 
basis of seafloor spreading data from the Indian 
ocean. These palaeomagnetic observations from the 
Cretaceous Takena Formation and the early Tertiary 
Lingzizong volcanics (Pozzi et al., 1982; Westphal et 
al., 1983; Westphal and Pozzi, 1983; Achache et al., 
1984; Lin and Watts, 1988) yield palaeolatitudes for 
the Lhasa block ranging from 6 up to 20°N. How- 
ever, according to Klootwijk et al. (1986, 1991) and 
Chen et al. (1993a), possible partial overprints limit 
the reliability of these data. A recently published 
Late Cretaceous pole (Chen et al., 1993a) indicates a 
palaeolatitude of 7°N for the southern margin of the 
Lhasa block. For the middle to Late Palaeocene 
Zongpu Formation we determined a palaeolatitude of 
4°N for the Tethyan Himalaya at Gamba. A palaeo- 
geographic reconstruction is shown in Fig. 16b. The 
position of stable India results from the mean of REF 
A and REF B. The northern margin of Greater India 
is drawn according to the mean value of observed 
palaeolatitudes from the Zongshan Formation and 
the Zongpu Formation, taking into account a decreas- 
ing magnitude of rotational shortening from east to 
west (700 km at Gamba, zero at pivot P; see Fig. 
16a). At the time of deposition of the Zongshan 
Formation there is still a wide oceanic gap between 
Greater India and Eurasia in the east. These data 
suggest that initial contact of Greater India and 
Eurasia has occurred close to the Cretaceous/Ter- 
tiary time boundary (65-60 Ma). A Late Palaeocene 
to Early Eocene age (55-50 Ma) is favoured for 
completion of suturing.
